original.q: When did you last change your smoke alarm batteries?
a: I took it down when it chirped
original.when: Once a year. Replace the whole alarm every 10 years.
original.why: Nearly 3 in 5 home fire deaths happen in homes where smoke alarms are missing or not working. Have 10-year sealed alarms? No batteries to change, just watch the date.
original.tip: Pick one date a year, like your birthday, and change them all at once.

revised.question: When did you last test your smoke alarms?

choices.text: Within the last month, including my sealed-battery alarms
A while ago. They’re due for a test
I took one down when it chirped

revised.rule: Test monthly. Follow the alarm’s instructions for battery care and whole-alarm replacement, generally at 10 years.
revised.why: An alarm needs to work when it counts. Sealed-battery models still need testing, but their batteries aren’t replaceable. Replace the whole unit at the end of its service life.
revised.tip: Check the date and test each alarm. If one is disconnected or won’t work, restore working protection promptly; ask your local fire department or a qualified installer for help.

original.q: When did you last change your furnace filter?
a: Totally forgot I needed to do this
original.when: At least every 90 days. More often if you have pets, heavy use, or a lot of dust.
original.why: A dirty, clogged filter can raise your AC’s energy use by 5% to 15%.
original.tip: Write the filter size down so the next store run takes two minutes.

revised.question: How are you keeping up with your furnace filter?

choices.text: I check it and follow my system’s schedule
Sometime this year. I should check the instructions
Totally forgot I needed to do this

revised.rule: Check it monthly. Clean or replace it on your filter and system’s schedule, sooner if it is dirty.
revised.why: A clogged filter restricts airflow and makes the system work harder. Filter type, dust, pets, and use can all change the schedule.
revised.tip: Save the filter size and your equipment’s instructions so the next store run is easier.

original.q: When was your dryer vent last cleaned out?
a: I thought the lint screen was the vent
original.when: Clean the vent once a year. Clear the lint screen every load.
original.why: Failure to clean is the leading cause of clothes dryer fires.
original.tip: If drying takes longer than it used to, the vent is likely clogged.

revised.question: When was your dryer vent last cleaned out?

choices.text: This year, and I follow the dryer’s instructions
I thought the lint screen was the vent

revised.rule: Clear the lint screen each load. Plan a yearly vent check and cleaning; follow the manual and act sooner if airflow drops.
revised.why: Lint buildup matters: failure to clean was the leading ignition factor in reported U.S. home dryer fires in 2018–2020.
revised.tip: Longer drying can signal restricted airflow, though there are other causes. Check the instructions and arrange qualified cleaning or service when needed.

source.name: U.S. Fire Administration: appliance fire safety

original.q: Have you ever cleaned your dishwasher filter?
a: In the last month or two
original.when: Every month or two. More often if you skip rinsing.
original.why: Spoiler: it’s probably gross. A clogged filter is a common reason “clean” dishes come out gritty or smelly.
original.tip: Twist it out from the bottom of the dishwasher and rinse it in warm, soapy water.

revised.question: How are you keeping up with your dishwasher filter?

choices.text: I follow the manual, including if mine is self-cleaning
Once, maybe. I should check its schedule

revised.rule: Check your manual. If yours has a removable filter, clean it on its schedule and reinstall it correctly.
revised.why: Spoiler: a neglected removable filter can get gross. Trapped food can leave dishes gritty or smelly. Some models clean their filters differently.
revised.tip: Find the model’s cleaning instructions before removing anything. There’s no one-size-fits-all twist-and-rinse routine.

original.q: How old is your water heater?
original.when: Know its age. Most last 10 to 15 years.
original.why: Knowing the age lets you replace it on your schedule, not after a leak floods the basement.
original.tip: Check the label on the tank for the date, then save it somewhere you’ll find it.

revised.question: How old is your water heater?
revised.rule: Know its age and type. Storage heaters often last 10 to 15 years; tankless can last over 20. Age isn’t a replacement deadline.
revised.why: Knowing its age helps you plan, without predicting a leak. Service life depends on the model, water conditions, care, and use.
revised.tip: Save the installation record or verify the manufacture date with the maker using the label and serial number. Those dates may differ.

source.name: U.S. Department of Energy: Energy Saver guide, water heating

original.q: Could you find the last pro who fixed something in your house?
a: I just Google a new one every time
original.when: Save the invoice, name, and number the day of the job.
original.why: 33% of homeowners say finding a reliable contractor is stressful. The good one is easy to lose.
original.tip: Snap the invoice before it disappears into a drawer.

revised.question: Could you find the last pro who fixed something in your house?

choices.text: I just Google a new one every time

revised.rule: Save the invoice, name, and number the day of the job.
revised.why: A good contractor is worth remembering. The good one is easy to lose when the invoice disappears into a drawer.
revised.tip: Snap the invoice before it disappears into a drawer.
